8. Game Theory

The grammar of strategic choice — from normal-form games and best responses through Nash equilibrium, mixed strategies, backward induction in dynamic games, and repeated games.

  • Normal-Form Games and Best Responses — Look directly at the 2×22 \times 22×2 payoff matrix. Mark player 1's best response in each column and player 2's in each row; the cells where both are bold — the starred cells — are exactly the pure-strategy Nash equilibria.
  • Mixed Strategies and the Indifference Condition — When player 2 mixes with probability qqq, player 1's expected payoff from each pure strategy is a line in qqq. At their crossing q∗q^*q∗ player 1 is indifferent — the only qqq that can appear in a mixed equilibrium.
  • Zero-Sum Games and Minimax — One player's gain is the other's loss. Edit the payoff matrix and compare maximin with minimax: equality means a saddle point (pure equilibrium); a gap means a fully mixed equilibrium and a value of the game.
  • Nash Equilibrium and Best-Response Correspondences — Draw both correspondences in the (q,p)(q, p)(q,p) plane: blue is player 1's optimal mix on qqq, orange is player 2's on ppp. Their intersections are the Nash equilibria — pure ones at the corners, the mixed one starred inside.
  • Iterated Elimination of Strictly Dominated Strategies — Delete what a rational player would never play, round by round. Push the round slider and C→M→DC \to M \to DC→M→D vanish in turn, until only UUU remains and player 2 answers with LLL.
  • Extensive-Form Games and Backward Induction — Draw the entry game as a tree. Push the slider to solve it backwards: the incumbent accommodates (111 beats −1-1−1), the entrant enters. The pruned Fight branch is a specimen of a non-credible threat.
  • Repeated Games and Cooperation — Play grim-trigger in the infinitely repeated Prisoner's Dilemma. Moving the discount factor δ\deltaδ flips which curve is on top — "always cooperate" vs "deviate once" — and cooperation survives in the shaded region right of δ∗=T−RT−P\delta^* = \frac{T-R}{T-P}δ∗=T−PT−R​.
